title: Mandela Writes to His Daughters from Prison
text:
Nelson Mandela was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964 and sent to Robben Island, off Cape Town. His two daughters with his wife Winnie, Zenani and Zindziswa, were small children at the time. Under prison rules, children under sixteen could not visit, and Mandela was allowed very few letters, all of them read by censors. Some of his letters never reached their destination.

In May 1969 Winnie was arrested and held in solitary confinement under the security laws. The girls, then eight and ten, were left without either parent at home. Mandela wrote to them from his cell. He told them that their mother had been taken away, that she was a brave woman who loved them and her people, and that one day they would be together again. He tried to explain to them, at a distance and through the censors, what was happening to their family, and to reassure them that they were not alone.

That same July, his eldest son, Thembekile, from his first marriage, was killed in a car accident. Mandela asked to attend the funeral and was refused.

He kept writing, to his children, his wife and others, for the rest of his twenty-seven years in prison. The letters were collected and published in 2018 as The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela. They show a father trying to stay present in his children's lives from a place where he could not reach them.
lesson: Even when we cannot be with our children, we can still reach them with words. Steady contact, however limited, tells a child they are not forgotten.
people: Nelson Mandela, Winnie Madikizela-Mandela, Zenani Mandela, Zindziswa Mandela
source: The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela, ed. Sahm Venter (2018)
